strengths: The paper targets an important and clinically motivated problem (visual prostheses) and proposes a concrete pipeline that combines a pretrained CLIP encoder with a cross-attention-conditioned DDPM for image-to-brain-signal generation.
The method is evaluated on two multimodal datasets (THINGS-EEG2 and THINGS-MEG) spanning both EEG and MEG, which is a reasonable attempt at demonstrating generality across signal modalities.

The ablation comparing cross-attention against addition and concatenation (Appendix A.1) is a sensible design choice, and the topography visualizations (Figures 3–8) provide an intuitive look at intra- and inter-subject variability.
The architecture and training setup (UNet2DConditionModel, channel dims, optimizer, batch sizes) are described with enough specificity that the method could in principle be reimplemented.
weaknesses: There is no comparison to any external baseline method. The paper repeatedly claims 'high-quality conversion' and that it 'advances the technical foundation,' yet it only ablates its own conditioning mechanism (cross-attention vs. addition vs. concatenation). The most similar prior work (Lu & Golomb, 2024) is discussed qualitatively but never compared quantitatively, so the central claim of superiority is unsupported.

The evaluation metrics are uninterpretable without reference levels. MSE and PCC to ground-truth signals are reported, but no trivial baselines (e.g., predicting the mean/zero signal, or a linear ridge regression) and no chance levels are given. For highly noisy M/EEG, a PCC of ~0.19 (EEG) and ~0.12 (MEG) could plausibly be near the noise floor, and MSE values (0.217, 0.763) cannot be judged without the data variance. This undermines the main empirical claim.

The ablation gains are marginal and may not be statistically meaningful. Cross-attention improves average MSE from 0.228 to 0.217 (EEG) and PCC from 0.180 to 0.188, while being worse than simpler conditioning for several individual subjects (e.g., EEG Subject 6: 0.247 cross-attention vs. 0.223 concatenation). No error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests are provided, so the 'consistent advantage' claim is not established.

The topography visualizations do not support image-specific generation. The generated topographies are averages over all stimuli per subject, which collapses to a generic evoked response and cannot demonstrate that different images produce different brain signals—the very capability needed to validate a brain-encoding model.

There is a conceptual mismatch between the stated application and the method. In a visual prosthesis, brain encoding maps images to electrode stimulation patterns, whereas this work maps images to recorded EEG/MEG signals (a neural-response prediction/forward-modeling task). The paper never closes the loop (e.g., showing that the predicted brain signals yield better stimuli or better phosphene/decoding outcomes), so the claimed relevance to improving visual prostheses is not demonstrated.

Novelty is incremental: the approach is essentially a standard DDPM with Stable-Diffusion-style cross-attention conditioning, applied to EEG/MEG regression. No new modeling insight or mechanism is introduced beyond the domain transfer.

The cross-subject analysis overreaches. Differences in source-model means are tiny (e.g., EEG MSE 0.195–0.246), and the conclusion that 'each subject exhibits inherent differences' is drawn from these small fluctuations without statistical support; the near-floor cross-subject PCC (~0.05–0.10) more plausibly indicates the model transfers little subject-specific information.

Reproducibility is only partial: preprocessing is deferred entirely to Song et al. (2025), and key diffusion details (number of sampling steps, noise schedule, conditioning at inference, evaluation protocol for PCC/MSE over time points) are not specified, making the reported numbers hard to reproduce or verify.

strengths: The paper addresses an interesting and potentially useful direction: image-to-brain signal generation using diffusion models.
It applies DDPM with cross-attention conditioning to both EEG and MEG generation and evaluates on two public multimodal datasets (THINGS-EEG2, THINGS-MEG) with multiple subjects.
It includes an ablation comparing cross-attention against addition/concatenation conditioning and provides topography visualizations across subjects.
The use of public datasets and standard metrics (MSE, PCC) makes the direction testable in principle.
weaknesses: The visual prosthesis motivation is conceptually flawed: in a prosthesis, brain encoding should map images to electrical stimulation patterns, not generate EEG/MEG. The paper conflates measured brain responses with stimulation and never evaluates phosphene or perceptual outcomes, so the claimed relevance to visual prostheses is unsupported.

There are no baseline comparisons: no comparison to prior image-to-EEG/MEG methods such as Lu & Golomb (2024), no regression or mean-predictor baseline, and no GAN or alternative generative baseline. The reported MSE/PCC values therefore cannot be interpreted.

Cross-attention is not a novel contribution; it is standard in conditional diffusion models. The ablation gains are marginal (e.g., EEG MSE 0.217 vs. 0.227/0.228; MEG PCC 0.122 vs. 0.118/0.109), with no statistical tests, confidence intervals, or error bars.
Biological plausibility is not established by MSE/PCC on raw M/EEG. No perceptual, phosphene, or neural-encoding metrics are used, and there is no comparison to actual prosthesis stimulation.

Cross-subject results are misinterpreted: small standard deviations across target subjects indicate consistent performance, not necessarily good generalization. Cross-subject PCC is much lower than within-subject (~0.104 EEG, ~0.054 MEG) and close to chance, contradicting the claim of good cross-subject generalization.

The evaluation protocol is ambiguous: it is unclear whether metrics are computed per test image or after averaging all generated signals across images. If averaged, the task is not image-to-brain mapping. Repetition handling and train/test splits are not fully specified.

Implementation details are insufficient for reproducibility: diffusion schedule/T, sampling steps, noise variance, random seeds, preprocessing details (only cites Song et al. 2025), ablation architecture details, and code are missing.

There is no ablation on the diffusion model itself (e.g., versus deterministic regression or a GAN) or on CLIP versus lower-level visual features, so the claims that DDPM and CLIP are beneficial are unsupported.

Topography visualizations show generated signals that visibly differ from real test signals, yet no quantitative spatial/temporal similarity analysis is provided. The visualizations are descriptive and do not validate the method.

The paper treats EEG/MEG as 2D image-like arrays (63x250, 271x200) with one channel without justifying whether this respects spatiotemporal structure or whether a 1D/sequential model would be more appropriate.

The limitations section only mentions compute constraints and omits fundamental limitations: no actual prosthesis validation, no baseline comparison, poor cross-subject transfer, and unclear biological relevance.
Presentation issues, including confusing terminology (brain encoding vs. brain signal generation), inconsistent capitalization, citation/date errors, and low-quality figures, reduce clarity.

The abstract and title overstate the contribution by claiming a visual prosthesis framework while the method is an offline image-to-EEG/MEG generator with no prosthesis or stimulus-encoding evaluation.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and under-explored direction: learning a mapping from images to human brain responses (EEG/MEG) using paired multimodal datasets, which is relevant to visual prostheses and brain encoding.

It provides a concrete pipeline combining CLIP visual features, a denoising diffusion probabilistic model, and cross-attention conditioning, with evaluations on two public datasets (THINGS-EEG2 and THINGS-MEG), demonstrating compatibility with both EEG and MEG signal dimensions.
An ablation study compares cross-attention conditioning against addition and concatenation, reporting average improvements on both datasets.
Topography visualizations across subjects give an intuitive view of intra- and inter-subject variability in EEG/MEG responses.
The problem formulation and standard DDPM training objective are clearly stated, making the overall architecture easy to follow.
The limitations section acknowledges computational constraints and the inability to test deeper architectures.
weaknesses: The central visual-prosthesis claim is unsupported: brain encoding in a prosthesis should map images to stimulation/phosphene patterns for an electrode array, not to EEG/MEG recordings. EEG/MEG are neural responses, not stimuli, so an image-to-EEG/MEG model does not directly solve the prosthetic stimulus-encoding problem. No phosphene model, electrode-array simulation, or downstream perceptual evaluation is provided.

The methodological novelty is limited: conditional DDPMs with cross-attention are standard components, and the paper does not introduce an EEG/MEG-specific diffusion process, architecture, or conditioning mechanism. Cross-attention is presented as the key innovation but is a well-known technique.

Cross-attention may be degenerate as described: h_img is described as a single CLIP embedding vector. With a single key/value token, softmax attention is uniform and cross-attention reduces to adding a global conditioning vector, contradicting the claimed 'fine-grained alignment' and 'dynamic interaction'. The paper does not specify whether patch tokens or multiple visual tokens are used.

No comparison is made to prior image-to-EEG/MEG generation methods such as Img2EEG, EEG-GAN, conditional GANs, regression baselines, or other diffusion models. The only ablation is addition vs. concatenation, and the gains are small and inconsistent across subjects (e.g., EEG subject 6 MSE 0.247 for cross-attention vs. 0.223 for concatenation; MEG subject 3 PCC 0.061 vs. 0.097 for addition).

Evaluation metrics and claims are weak: MSE/PCC against ground-truth signals do not establish biological plausibility, and PCC values are low (EEG ~0.19, MEG ~0.12, cross-subject ~0.05-0.10). There are no statistical tests, no distributional/generative evaluation, no quantitative topography or spectral comparison, and no downstream utility measure.

The cross-subject generalization claim is misleading: small standard deviations across target subjects for a source model can reflect consistently poor transfer rather than good generalization. Cross-subject PCC drops substantially compared with within-subject results, and this degradation is not adequately addressed.

Reproducibility is insufficient: no code, no diffusion scheduler details, noise schedule, number of diffusion steps, CLIP feature type (pooled vs. token sequence), seeds, normalization, or full preprocessing details. Preprocessing is only cited to Song et al. (2025).

Visualization evidence is qualitative and partly misaligned: generated topographies visibly differ from real test topographies, and difference maps compare training vs. test rather than generated vs. test, so they do not validate generation quality.

Ethical and clinical implications of visual prostheses are not discussed, including safety, informed consent, risk of misleading neural signal generation, and data governance. There is no code/data availability statement.

strengths: Addresses an under-explored direction: image-to-brain (encoding) generation as a complement to the heavily studied brain-decoding pipeline for visual prostheses, which is a reasonable and novel framing.

The proposed framework coherently integrates several components—a DDIM-based Diffusion Transformer, cross-attention alignment with concatenated CLIP image + text embeddings, LLM-generated captions, and a learnable spatio-temporal position embedding—and the architecture is clearly described with figures and pseudocode.

Evaluation is performed on two multimodal benchmarks (THINGS-EEG2 and THINGS-MEG) under both within-subject and cross-subject settings, with component ablations and a brain-region ablation that yields a neuroscientifically sensible finding (occipital region contributes most).
The appendix provides reasonably detailed preprocessing, dataset descriptions, hyperparameters, and training/inference algorithms, which supports partial reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central claim of generating 'biologically plausible' signals is not adequately supported by the evaluation. MSE/Pearson/Cosine/SL between generated and ground-truth signals can be inflated by regression to the mean; crucially, there is no trivial baseline (e.g., predicting the training-set mean response, or per-image averaged responses) or noise-ceiling comparison, so it is unclear whether the model genuinely predicts stimulus-driven structure or simply outputs an average response.

The within-subject Pearson correlations (e.g., 0.425 for EEG) are implausibly high relative to typical single-trial EEG encoding performance in the literature, and they are internally inconsistent with the much lower cross-subject values (0.157 EEG, 0.082 MEG). This discrepancy raises concerns about the evaluation setup (e.g., averaged targets, leakage, or metric inflation) and is not explained.

The baseline comparison is weak and not well matched to the task. Traditional linear encoding models (Güçlü, Yamins) and an fMRI-specific VAE (SynBrain) do not represent strong or appropriate generative/encoding baselines; there is no comparison to standard conditional generative models (VAE/GAN), to a simple conditional MLP regressor, or to a nearest-neighbor retrieval of training brain responses. There is also no DDPM-vs-DDIM ablation despite DDIM being a stated design choice.

The connection to visual prostheses is overstated. The brain encoding stage of a prosthesis must produce stimulation patterns for an electrode array; generating M/EEG does not directly yield such stimuli, and no downstream phosphene/percept evaluation is performed. The stated practical utility is therefore not demonstrated.

Methodological novelty is limited: DiT, DDIM, cross-attention, CLIP embeddings, and learnable position embeddings are all standard components applied to a new task, and the LLM-caption contribution is marginal (removing CLIP text embeddings changes MSE only from 0.109 to 0.117), which is small relative to the added pipeline complexity.

No statistical significance testing across subjects/participants is reported, so it is unclear whether the reported improvements over baselines are meaningful given the small number of subjects (10 EEG, 4 MEG).
Some presentation issues (inconsistent figure rendering, apparent citation/labeling artifacts in the reference list) reduce clarity.

strengths: The paper targets an under-explored and potentially valuable direction: image-to-brain signal generation (the encoding direction) rather than the more heavily studied decoding direction, and it evaluates on two established multimodal benchmarks (THINGS-EEG2 and THINGS-MEG).

The proposed pipeline is coherent and internally consistent: a DiT/DDIM backbone conditioned via cross-attention on concatenated CLIP image and LLM-caption text embeddings, plus additive brain-region and temporal embeddings.

The paper includes component ablations (text embeddings, region embeddings, temporal embeddings) and a brain-region ablation whose finding that the occipital region dominates is at least qualitatively consistent with known visual-cortex function.
The manuscript is reasonably organized, and the appendices provide preprocessing and architectural detail (patch sizes, channel groupings, DDIM formulations).
weaknesses: The central claim of generating 'biologically plausible' brain signals is not adequately supported. Evaluation relies exclusively on signal-similarity metrics (MSE, Pearson, cosine, Synchronization Likelihood) between generated and ground-truth signals. There is no decoding-based evaluation (e.g., top-k image identification/retrieval from the generated signals), which is the standard test of whether encoded/generated signals carry the correct information. SL is a weak and indirect proxy for biological plausibility, and the claim that signals are 'biologically plausible' is essentially asserted rather than demonstrated.

The application framing is conceptually flawed. EEG/MEG are recording modalities; the paper repeatedly describes them as 'evoking visual percepts' and as the 'brain decoding stage' of a visual prosthesis, conflating recording with stimulation. A visual prosthesis pipeline requires predicting stimulation patterns for an electrode array, and generating EEG from images does not directly serve that goal. No downstream experiment shows that the generated signals improve any prosthesis-related outcome.

Baselines are weak and the comparison is likely unfair. The non-generative baselines (Güçlü et al. 2015; Yamins et al. 2014) are 2014-2015 CNN-feature + linear-regression encoding models and do not represent the current state of the art for EEG/MEG encoding (e.g., NICE, ATM, EEG2Image-style models are not compared). The only modern baseline, SynBrain, was designed for fMRI and is said to be 'adapted' to M/EEG, but no adaptation details, hyperparameters, or tuning are provided, undermining both fairness and reproducibility.

There is no statistical rigor. No confidence intervals, standard deviations, or significance tests are reported, despite 'averaged over ten subjects/four participants' being mentioned. The reported gains over SynBrain (e.g., Pearson 0.425 vs 0.366 on EEG) and the ablation deltas (e.g., THINGS-MEG Pearson 0.379 vs 0.361 without text embeddings) are small and may not be statistically significant.

Metric definitions and computation are underspecified, limiting reproducibility and interpretability: it is unclear whether correlations/cosine are computed per-sample and then averaged or on condition-averaged responses, and the units/scale of the MSE are unclear given MVNN whitening. Without this, the absolute numbers (e.g., MSE 0.109) cannot be interpreted.

Cross-subject performance is markedly worse and is acknowledged, yet cross-subject generalization is essential for any real prosthesis application (one cannot retrain per patient). The paper nonetheless claims broad usefulness for visual prostheses, which the within-subject setup does not support.

Reproducibility is a concern: no code or model release is indicated, baseline training details are absent, the SynBrain adaptation is undocumented, and key sampling/training hyperparameters (e.g., DDIM steps, noise schedule specifics beyond 'linear') are incomplete.

Originality is limited. DiT + cross-attention + CLIP conditioning is a standard combination, and conditioning on LLM-generated captions is an established technique. The 'learnable spatio-temporal position encoding' reduces to two learned embedding tables added together and is an incremental contribution rather than a novel mechanism.

The CLIP-score analysis is not very informative: reporting that 98.7% of captions fall in the 0.6-0.8 range (with CLIP scores generally being high) does not establish that the captions contribute semantically meaningful conditioning, nor does it validate caption quality for this task.
Minor presentation issues (e.g., inconsistent citation formatting in the reference list) further reduce clarity.

strengths: The paper tackles an under-explored and practically relevant direction: the brain-encoding stage (image→brain signal) of the visual prosthesis pipeline, which is indeed much less studied than brain decoding.

The method is coherent and reasonably well-engineered: a DiT/DDIM backbone with cross-attention conditioning on CLIP image + LLM-caption text embeddings, plus a learnable spatio-temporal (region + temporal) position encoding tailored to M/EEG.

The empirical study is broad for a paper of this scope: two datasets (THINGS-EEG2, THINGS-MEG), within- and cross-subject settings, component-wise ablations (CLIP text, region, temporal embeddings), an LLM comparison, and a brain-region ablation that yields a neuroscience-consistent finding (occipital region most important).

The brain-region ablation (occipital removal degrades performance most) is a nice sanity check that aligns with known visual cortex function, and the use of the nonlinear Synchronization Likelihood metric goes beyond simple correlation.

Reproducibility is partially supported: the appendix specifies architecture hyperparameters (hidden dim, layers, heads, patch size, timesteps), optimizer settings, and detailed preprocessing for both datasets, which is more than many comparable papers provide.
weaknesses: The central motivating claim—advancing visual prostheses via more 'biologically plausible' brain signals—is not validated. No phosphene model or downstream perceptual/decoding evaluation is used, so there is no evidence that the generated signals actually improve the prosthesis pipeline. The paper only shows similarity to recorded signals, which is a much weaker claim than 'biologically plausible.'

The baselines are weak and the comparison is not compelling. The main competitors are classical encoding models from 2014–2015 (Güçlü & Van Gerven; Yamins et al.) that use CNN features plus linear regression, and SynBrain, which was designed for fMRI and is merely adapted here. No modern EEG/MEG generation or encoding baselines are included, so the SOTA claim is not well supported.

The evaluation protocol is ambiguous in a way that materially affects interpretation. The test set has 200 concepts × 80 repetitions (EEG) and 200 × 12 (MEG); it is never clearly stated whether metrics are computed on single trials or on trial-averaged responses. If averaged, the reported Pearson ≈ 0.42 for EEG substantially overstates single-trial generation capability, which is the practically relevant regime. This needs to be explicit.

No uncertainty quantification. Results are 'averaged over ten subjects' / 'four participants' but no variance, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported, making it hard to judge whether the (often small) improvements over ablations and baselines are reliable.

Novelty is modest. DiT + DDIM with cross-attention conditioning on CLIP embeddings, LLM-generated captions, and learnable positional embeddings are all standard, off-the-shelf components; the contribution is essentially an application/combination of existing ideas to a new data modality, which the framing as a 'novel framework' oversells.

Cross-subject results are essentially non-functional (Pearson 0.157 for EEG, 0.082 for MEG), which the paper reports honestly but does not analyze; this severely limits practical utility (a per-subject training session would be required) and undercuts the prosthesis narrative, yet it is not discussed as a limitation of the approach itself.

Several presentation issues: Figure 1's caption/text does not match the depicted image, some figure content is low quality, and there are minor mathematical/typographical inconsistencies (e.g., the DDIM update presentation and the patch-count arithmetic).

Reproducibility gaps remain: no code/weights release is indicated, seeds and the exact number of trained models are unspecified, and the caption-generation and embedding pipeline at test time is not fully pinned down.
